title: Rory and Maple's Quarry Climb
markdown:
Rory the rook had feathers as dark as midnight and eyes sharp enough to spot a worm from a mile high. But Rory had a secret: his heart fluttered like a butterfly whenever he looked down from a great height. He would flap with all his might, yet his courage often seemed to tangle at the edge of the sky.

Close by, where the old quarry yawned like a sleeping dragon’s maw, lived a mini giantess named Maple. Maple was as strong as ten oxen; her hands could move boulders with a gentle push. Yet she often felt clumsy, fearing her footsteps might crumble the world or her laughter shake the stars. She longed to be delicate, to tiptoe like a dewdrop.

One breezy afternoon, as the sun painted apricot and rose, a faint sad sound drifted from the quarry. Bleat. Bleat. A lost and frightened sheep.

Rory, perched on a fence post, tilted his head. Maple, tending her giant-sized garden, paused mid-dig, enormous hands hovering over shimmering moonflowers.

“That sounds like Daisy,” Maple rumbled, pebbles down a gentle hill. “She’s wandered too close to the quarry again. Oh dear.”

Rory’s heart gave a little lurch, the familiar uncomfortable flutter. The quarry. So high. So deep. He imagined the dizzying drop. The bleating grew more desperate. He looked at Maple. She looked at him, earnest eyes wide.

“We must help her,” Maple said, setting down her enormous spade. A soft thud.

Rory puffed his chest, trying to still the flutter. He flapped once, twice, a small determined gesture. “Yes,” he croaked, steadier than he expected. “We must.”

The journey was short. The climb up the sheer face was another matter. Walls rose, imposing. Rory knew he should fly up with ease, but his wings felt heavy, fear a leaden weight. Maple, strong enough to scramble, worried about dislodging loose stones.

“Don’t worry, little one,” Maple whispered, seeing his unease. “I will go slowly. And you can guide me with your sharp eyes. You know this land best from above.”

And so they began. Rory, despite trembling, hopped and flapped upward, keen eyes scanning for safe handholds. Maple followed, movements surprisingly careful, mighty hands gripping stone with a precision that belied her size.

As they climbed, Rory noticed something extraordinary etched into the walls: stripes. Bands of rich red, cool grey, and creamy white, stacked one upon another, like countless pages in a gigantic ancient book.

“Look, Maple,” he croaked. Fear forgotten for a moment. “The rocks. They are like layers. So many colours.”

Maple paused, gaze following his pointed beak. “My grandfather told me the world is very, very old. These layers took so, so long to form. Each one a story of a different time.”

Higher. The bleating grew louder, tinged with panic. There, on a narrow ledge, was Daisy, wool snagged tightly on a thorny bush. She trembled, unable to move.

Rory felt a surge of resolve. For Daisy. For Maple. He flew closer, wings beating steadily now, light with purpose. “Hold on, Daisy. We’re here. We’ll get you down.”

He turned to Maple, sharp eyes assessing. “The bush is strong. But its roots are shallow. If you can pull just so—gently—you might loosen it without disturbing the rock too much.”

Maple understood. She reached out, giant fingers surprisingly delicate. She tested the rock, found a stable spot, and with a mighty yet controlled heave, shifted the stone. The thorny bush loosened. A final careful tug, and Daisy was free.

Rory then guided them both down. His wings felt lighter with every strong steady flap. The wind rushed past, not with fear, but with exhilaration.

Back on solid ground, Daisy shook herself and trotted toward her meadow with a relieved baa, thankful in Rory’s direction. Rory looked up at the towering quarry. Its walls now seemed less a threat than a magnificent layered sculpture. He had flown higher than he thought possible.

Maple, who had always feared her tremendous strength would cause harm, knew in the warmth of her hands that she could be both immensely powerful and remarkably gentle.

“You were very brave, Rory,” Maple said, soft as a summer breeze.

“And you were very strong, Maple,” Rory replied. His heart beat with a steady confident rhythm. “And those stripes in the rock… they show that even great things take time to build, layer by layer.”

They promised to explore the quarry again, not with fear, but with the thrill of discovery. The oldest stone held. Daisy’s bleat faded into ordinary grass. Maple’s spade waited by the moonflowers, and Rory, for the first time, looked down from the fence post on purpose.
